'''''Heliotropium angiospermum''''', common name '''scorpion's tail''' or '''scorpion-tail''', is a flowering plant in the ''[[Heliotropium]]'' genus and family [[Heliotropiaceae]]. An annual or short-lived perennial<ref name=fm>{{Cite web|url=https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/wildflowers/flowers/scorpion-tail/|title=Scorpion-tail|website=Florida's Wildflowers & Butterflies}}</ref> it grows in Florida and Texas<ref name=wf/> into Mexico<ref name=mex/> as well as on various islands in arid lowlands.<ref>{{Cite book |last=McMullen |first=Conley K. |title=Flowering Plants of the Galápagos |date=2018 |isbn=978-1-5017-2876-1 |location=Ithaca, NY |oclc=1102799994|page=180}}</ref> Its nectar is sought-out by butterflies<ref name="wf">{{Cite web|url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=hean5|title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin|website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref> and also provides food for bees and birds.<ref name=wf/> The stems terminate in [[wiktionary:scorpioid|scorpioid]] inflorescences.<ref name="mex">{{Cite book |last=Eason |first=Michael |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UZQ0DwAAQBAJ&dq=wildflowers+of+texas+eason+Heliotropium+angiospermum&pg=PA112 |title=Wildflowers of Texas |date=2018 |publisher=Timber Press, Incorporated |isbn=978-1-60469-862-6 |location=North Adams |page=112 |oclc=1022795434}}</ref>

It is employed for medicinal uses on some Caribbean islands.<ref name="wf"/><ref>{{Cite book |last=Dehgan |first=Bijan |title=Garden plants taxonomy. Volume 2, Angiosperms (eudicots) |date=2023 |isbn=978-3-031-11565-3 |location=Cham |oclc=1376018172|page=941}}</ref>

It can tolerate rocky or sandy soil and grows up to 3-feet high.<ref name=fm/>
